summary: The note describes how energy companies are reassessing preparedness for space weather after recent geomagnetic disturbances, citing a September 4, 2023 solar flare that disrupted Northern European grids and a September 17, 2023 storm in New Hampshire. Experts outline mitigation strategies: hardening infrastructure, better forecasting, operational protocols, R&D, collaboration, workforce training, and public awareness. The takeaway is that a multifaceted approach combining technology, investment and international cooperation is needed.
one_line: Energy companies are adopting multifaceted strategies, from GIC-blocking hardware to forecasting and training, to protect power grids from solar flares and geomagnetic storms.
key_facts: On September 4, 2023, a substantial solar flare disrupted power networks in Northern Europe.
On September 17, 2023, a geomagnetic storm triggered by a potent CME exposed vulnerabilities in power transmission lines in New Hampshire, causing voltage regulation anomalies lasting hours.
Michael Durand, incident manager at New England Electric, said the storm had a domino effect, overloading transformers and leading to rolling blackouts.
Space weather includes solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and high-speed solar wind streams that can cause geomagnetic storms.
Dr. Emily Stanton of the National Space Weather Program said solar flares emit x-rays and ultraviolet radiation that affect the ionosphere and disrupt long-range radio communications.
James Kinsey of the Resilient Grid Initiative said companies are using GIC (Geomagnetically Induced Current) blocking devices to protect transformers during solar storms.
Veronica Hughes of the Space Weather Prediction Center said satellite data and collaboration with space agencies help forecast impacts and adjust grid operations.
Paul Jensen of American Power & Light said protocols include rerouting power loads and suspending non-critical maintenance during solar storm warnings.
A consortium of European energy firms has funded a multi-year research initiative to develop new materials and technologies protecting against geomagnetic disturbances.
Sandra Lee, a grid security expert, said utilities attend international symposiums and share best practices through a network of providers.
Richard Thomson of SolarGuard Power Corp. said staff from frontline technicians to top executives undergo specialized solar storm training.
Energy companies are also educating customers about solar-related service disruptions and how to prepare for outages.
